titleStmt.title: Pfairness applied to EDF to reduce migration overheads and improve task schedulability in multicore platforms

analytic.title: Pfairness applied to EDF to reduce migration overheads and improve task schedulability in multicore platforms

div.p: This paper proposes a scheduler combining the concepts of EDF and pfairness using the worst fit heuristic function. In scheduling algorithms without pfairness, priority is not monitored closely in case of preemptions. An algorithm combining EDF and pfairness proposed in this paper overcomes this drawback. Here resources are granted in accordance to the task weight. Individually using either EDF or pfairness utilizes the resources to a greater extent, whereas a combination of both achieves better reduction in migration overheads. The algorithm has been simulated on Cheddar, a real time scheduling tool, and also on SESC, an architectural simulator on multicore platforms. The algorithm presented in this paper has been tested for 5000 random task sets. The results show that it reduces the migration overhead by 33% for partitioned task sets and by 38 % for hybrid task sets, and improves task schedulability by 37%, compared to conventional EDF.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Multiprocessor systems primarily use three different scheduling approaches, namely, partitioned, global and hybrid. In partitioned scheduling, task migrations are totally restricted, resulting in increased overheads in cases of preemption, as explained by Sun et al in [1]. Global scheduling, on the other hand, permits task migration fully. This results in increase in migration overheads, even in the absence of preemption, as discussed by Moir and Ramamurthy in [2]. Hybrid scheduling combines the features of partitioned and global, where task migration is permitted in a restricted manner, which is better than partitioned and global approaches.

The above approaches, namely, partitioned, global and hybrid are applied to scheduling algorithms like EDF (Earliest Deadline First), to add restrictions to the system for obtaining feasible schedules. In the absence of these approaches, it is not possible to visualise and handle exceptions like task preemption. In EDF, tasks are scheduled according to their precedence constraints, but their priority is not closely monitored in cases of preemption. Quantum intervals are defined for monitoring the migration overheads. EDF scheduling incurs a larger migration overhead at the quantum interval (-γ) to (+ γ), where γ is a parameter indicating execution queue overhead, as discussed by Holman and Anderson in [3]. Migration overheads increase rapidly at the point (γ / 2) in the above interval.

Further in each method, the concept of fairness has been introduced, to execute tasks in proportion to their priority. There are many fairness scheduling strategies, like ER fair, PD 2 fair, and pfair. All these can be applied to the EDF algorithm. Previously ER fair and PD 2 fair have been applied to EDF algorithm. The following drawbacks were encountered. In ER fair, all tasks are given fairness by making them eligible for execution even before they are actually eligible, as explained by Calandrino et al in [4]. This results in more tasks producing larger migration overhead on the system, as all tasks that are eligible demand fairness from the scheduler. On the other hand, on application of PD 2 fair, a pseudo deadline is created and tasks are scheduled accordingly. But this again sets a false alarm indication to schedule tasks based on a pseudo deadline, even when the actual deadline has not arrived, as discussed by Anderson and Srinivasan in [5]. This can result in a critical task missing its deadline.

Pfairness is a fairness approach by which fairness is granted proportionate to the priority. A task of least priority is not given more fairness by the scheduler and vice versa. In pfair scheduling, the precedence constraints are not closely monitored while scheduling the tasks. Pfair scheduling incurs a larger migration overhead in the quantum interval (-cγ/2) to (+cγ/2), where c is the average number of jobs and γ is the start time of execution. Migration overheads are maximum at (cγ/4) due to absence of precedence constraints, as discussed by Anderson and Jonsson in [6].
To include pfairness, a heuristic function is needed to set a clear cut objective, as explained by Baruah in [7].

Commonly known heuristic functions are best fit, first fit, next fit and worst fit. Of the above, best fit, first fit and next fit are mostly applied to EDF scheduling, as explained by Anderson et al in [8]. In a multicore platform, these heuristic functions schedule tasks on each core, based on the scheduling constraints defined for that core. They do not update the current situation, if an external task arrives due to preemption or if any exceptions are encountered. But worst fit heuristic function takes care of such exceptions and updates the schedule according to the prevailing situation. This work combines the features of EDF and pfairness using worst fit heuristic function and proposes a new scheduling algorithm to monitor precedence constraints and ensure fairness to tasks according to their priority even in exceptional conditions. The migration overheads are incurred in the interval from -(γ+cα/2) to +(γ +cα/2), where α is the starting time of tasks entering the queue, γ is the queue overhead and c is the average number of tasks. The average migration overhead on using conventional EDF for partitioned task sets using 4 cores is 34.49 and those for hybrid task sets using 4 cores, and 16 cores are 32.27 and 96.74 respectively as explained by Calandrino et al in [4].

By combining the features of EDF and pfairness not only fairness is granted but also a portion of resources is reserved for future scheduling. This enables the minimization of overhead and workload on the scheduler. The optimization constraints on the scheduler are also closely monitored. In case these constraints get modified under exceptional conditions, the scheduler addresses these issues by recomputing the priorities and actual task utilisations. The migration overhead gets optimised in proportion to the resources actually utilized by the tasks.

A real time scheduling tool Cheddar has been used for monitoring the migration overheads, as discussed by Signhoff and Plantec in [9] and [10]. To check the task schedulability SESC, an architectural simulator has been used, as discussed by Montesinos Ortego and Sack in [11] and [12].

The algorithm presented in this paper has been tested for 5000 random task sets. The results show that it reduces the migration overhead by 33% for partitioned task sets and by 38 % for hybrid task sets, and improves task schedulability by 37%, compared to conventional EDF.

The paper is organized as follows: Section II discusses the algorithm, with an example. Section III discusses the simulation results from Cheddar and SESC for the algorithm in multicore platforms. Section IV concludes the work and presents the scope for future work.

div.head: II. ALGORITHM
div.p: The steps of the algorithm are outlined below: • Compute weight for task as weight=((quantum slice time/total allocated time by scheduler) *total processing time by core for the particular task). As a proof of concept the working of this algorithm for an example task set is presented below.

div.head: A Example
div.p: A task set comprising of 6 tasks is assumed to be scheduled on 3 cores. The tasks are intra-sporadic with a weight of 4/7 each. Table 1 indicates execution time, arrival time and the deadline of each task. The algorithm is simulated using Cheddar. It facilitates monitoring preemptions, context switchings, and migration overheads. The overloaded cores along with the resource allocation constraints are identified. The tool also monitors the utilisation bounds for partitioned and hybrid task sets.

The initial schedule without optimality check is developed using EDF strategy. Later, optimization is carried out, so that no core remains idle. Then, pfairness is applied by computing the lag. Lag is the difference between the scheduler allocated time and the actual utilised time for each task. Overloaded cores are identified and migrations are carried out where necessary. The algorithm has been tested for different task sets and the results are provided in the next section.

div.head: A Migration overheads
div.p: The algorithm has been implemented in Cheddar for 5000 random task sets of various types like partitioned task sets on 4 cores (vide Table II), hybrid task sets in 4 cores (vide table III) and hybrid task sets in 16 cores (vide table IV) respectively. Migration overheads are computed for system utilisations of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%, against task utilisations of 1/10, 1/5, 1/3, ½, and 1, for each core respectively. In table II for partitioned task sets on 4 cores, it is observed that the migration overhead is reduced from 34.49 for conventional EDF to 23.22 for EDF combined with pfairness approach, thus reducing migration overhead by 33%. Columns indicating NA signify that there are no migrations at that particular system and task utilisation. In table III for hybrid task sets on 4 cores, it is observed that the migration overhead is reduced from 32.27 for conventional EDF to 22.57 for EDF combined with pfairness approach, thus reducing migration overhead by 26%. In table IV, for hybrid task sets on 16 cores, it is observed that the migration overhead is reduced from 96.74 for conventional EDF to 60.20 for EDF combined with pfairness approach, thus reducing migration overhead by 38%.

The reduction in migration overhead for hybrid task sets is 26% for 4 cores and 38 % for 16 cores. As such, there is a greater reduction in migration overhead with increase in number of cores when pfairness is applied to EDF.
It is observed from the simulation results, that pfairness applied to EDF reduces migration overhead by 33% for partitioned task sets, and 38% for hybrid task sets.

div.head: B Task schedulability
div.p: Task schedulability for the algorithm, as measured by the number of tasks scheduled has been analysed using both Cheddar and SESC and results are tabulated in table V and VI respectively. Table VI using SESC indicates that the number of tasks scheduled increases from 398 for conventional EDF to 532 for EDF combined with pfairness approach, indicating an improvement of 36%.
These results indicate that pfairness when applied to EDF improves task schedulability by 37 %.

div.head: IV CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: In this paper, a new scheduler has been proposed combining the concepts of EDF and pfairness. It is observed that the concept of pfairness when applied to EDF, reduces the migration overhead by 33% for partitioned task sets and by 38 % for hybrid task sets, and improves task schedulability by 37%, compared to conventional EDF.

Work can be further extended to incorporate the concept of non-uniform laxity for obtaining results similar to static scheduling techniques. Other fairness strategies like ER fair and PD 2 fair can also be used to optimise overheads like context switching and preemption.
